**Evidence**
- CO2 mole fraction. Test condition recorded in PSI tables (-). FLEX: 274 values, 0–0.7 -. [S10]
- Helium mole fraction. Test condition recorded in PSI tables (-). FLEX: 274 values, 0–0.45 -; CFI: 87 values, 0–0.59 -. [S11]

- FLEX: The primary hypothesis of the FLEX mission is that microgravity conditions fundamentally alter the combustion and extinction characteristics of liquid fuel droplets due to changes in species and energy transport dynamics, radiative heat loss, and chemical kinetics.… [S5]
- Dust can look like smoke to a particle counter: DAFT showed that a modified commercial particle counter could be used in microgravity, measuring a test dust aerosol released on the ISS. Limitation: Terrestrial test dust, not lunar regolith; feasibility test only. [S12]
- BASS-II maps solid-fuel burning down to 13.6 % O2: BASS-II ran 129 tests with initial O2 between 13.6 and 22.2 % vol, mostly on PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric), Nomex. Flow annotations record extinction in 15 tests, blow-off in 3 and no ignition in 1. Limitation: Outcome annotations  [S13]

sources.title: FLEX — Flame Extinguishment Experiment — hypothesis
sources.text: The primary hypothesis of the FLEX mission is that microgravity conditions fundamentally alter the combustion and extinction characteristics of liquid fuel droplets due to changes in species and energy transport dynamics, radiative heat loss, and chemical kinetics. Specifically, the hypothesis posits that the lack of buoyant convection in microgravity will lead to significant differences in the flammability limits and suppression efficacy of various fire suppressant agents compared to normal gravity conditions. This hypothesis underpins the design of the FLEX experiments, which aim to map flammability boundaries, quantify suppressant efficacy, and develop predictive models to improve fire safety in space environments.

sources.title: FLEX — Flame Extinguishment Experiment — researchImpacts
sources.text: The mission's findings on the effectiveness of various fire suppressants, including CO2, He, and SF6, in microgravity can lead to the development of more efficient and less harmful fire suppression systems, reducing the risk of toxic byproducts during fire events. Additionally, the study of ''cool flames'' and low-temperature combustion processes observed in microgravity can inform the design of advanced combustion engines, leading to improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions in automotive and industrial applications. Overall, the FLEX mission's contributions to combustion science have the potential to enhance both space exploration safety and terrestrial fire safety technologies.

sources.title: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets — researchImpacts
sources.text: This study sought to enhance understanding of soot formation, flame structure, and radiative transport under microgravity and normal gravity, improving predictive models for combustion in both spacecraft and terrestrial systems. For space applications, the results support safer fire detection, suppression, and cleaner combustion technologies critical for long-duration missions. On Earth, the insights help reduce pollutant emissions, optimize combustion efficiency, and inform the design of cleaner energy and industrial systems.

sources.title: Cool flames: combustion at 500–1000 K
sources.text: Cool diffusion flames have peak temperatures of about 500–1000 K. FLEX, CFI and CFI-G studied them on droplets and burners in microgravity. Limitation: Research fuels and configurations; relevance to cabin fires is an open question, not a finding.

sources.title: More oxygen: droplet flames more often survive to burnout
sources.text: FLEX droplet tests in N2-only atmospheres that ended in flame extinction before burnout — Heptane: 5/17 at 21 % O2 vs 0/11 at 30–34 % O2; Methanol: 9/12 at 21 % O2 vs 2/13 at 30–34 % O2. Remaining tests ended in burnout ('completion') or droplet disruption. Limitation: Isolated droplets, two fuels; 'extinction' here means the flame went out before the droplet was consumed (often radiative), not the action of an extinguisher. Counts, not a model.

top_passage.text: Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in such systems is critical in the modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which soot formation and radiative transfer take place. In addition, an understanding of those factors that affect flame extinction in diffusion flames is critical in the suppression of fires and in improving engine efficiency. While normal gravity combustion studies can provide important information on combustion processes, the effects of gravitational forces often complicate the interpretation of both computational and experimental results.

top_passage.text: External thermo-convective perturbations (imposed temperature gradients, non-uniform heating, oscillatory/shear inflow) were expected to govern cool-flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition, and extinction by shifting residence time and scalar dissipation. In microgravity, where buoyancy was suppressed, this forcing was anticipated to dominate transport. A multidimensional, multi-physics CFD model was used to map perturbation-dependent stability boundaries and predict observables for comparison with FLEX data.
